title: What a CDN solves (latency, scale, and origin shielding)
hook: When a user in Tokyo loads your app hosted in Virginia, every asset crosses the Pacific unless something caches it closer. A Content Delivery Network (CDN) stores copies at edge locations so repeat requests never reach your origin region.

blocks.text: A Content Delivery Network (CDN) is a geographically distributed set of caches — Points of Presence (PoPs) — that sit between users and your origin servers. On a cache hit the edge responds locally. On a miss the edge fetches from origin once, stores the response, and serves subsequent users from that PoP. Amazon CloudFront is AWS's CDN; Akamai, Cloudflare, and Fastly solve the same class of problem on other clouds.

entries.plainDefinition: Distributed cache network that serves content from locations near the user.
entries.example: CloudFront edge in Mumbai serves app.js without a round trip to us-east-1.

entries.plainDefinition: A physical edge site where the CDN keeps caches and serves traffic.
entries.example: CloudFront has 600+ PoPs worldwide as of AWS documentation.

entries.plainDefinition: The authoritative source the CDN fetches from on a cache miss.
entries.example: Private S3 bucket, ALB, or API Gateway behind the distribution.

entries.plainDefinition: Edge already has the object and returns it without contacting origin.
entries.example: Second user in Singapore gets main.a3f2.js from local edge — X-Cache: Hit.

blocks.text: Latency is distance plus round trips. A 200 ms cross-ocean hop per asset multiplies across dozens of files. CDNs also absorb traffic spikes — viral posts hit edge caches instead of melting your single-region ALB. They add a DDoS absorption layer (especially with AWS Shield on CloudFront). The tradeoff: you must only cache responses that are safe to repeat — static assets, public GETs — never personalized POST bodies or auth-gated JSON unless the cache key includes the user identity.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: CDN moves bytes closer and reduces origin load. It is not a database, not a load balancer replacement for stateful writes, and not magic — cacheability rules still apply.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: DNS resolves to nearest edge
items.body: User requests https://app.example.com/assets/logo.png. DNS returns a CloudFront edge IP based on latency routing.

items.title: Edge checks local cache
items.body: CloudFront computes a cache key from path, query string, and configured headers/cookies.

items.title: Cache miss fetches origin
items.body: Edge contacts S3 or your custom origin in the home region, streams the object, stores it, returns to user.

items.title: Cache hit on repeat
items.body: Another user in the same PoP region gets the object from edge RAM/disk — origin sees zero additional requests.

diagram.title: CDN cache hit and miss
diagram.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant E as Edge PoP
  participant O as Origin S3
  U->>E: GET /assets/app.js
  alt cache HIT
    E-->>U: 200 from edge
  else cache MISS
    E->>O: GET object
    O-->>E: 200 + body
    E-->>U: 200 + store copy
  end

snippet.label: CLI — measure latency with and without CDN
snippet.code:
# Direct to S3 website endpoint (no CDN) — note Server and timing
curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'time_total: %{time_total}s\n' \
  https://my-bucket.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/assets/app.js

# Through CloudFront distribution domain
curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'time_total: %{time_total}s\n' \
  https://d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net/assets/app.js

# Second request — should show X-Cache: Hit from cloudfront
curl -sI https://d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net/assets/app.js | grep -i x-cache
snippet.explanation: First curl hits origin region directly. Second goes through edge DNS. Repeat request inspects X-Cache header — Hit means CDN saved an origin round trip.

snippet.label: CloudFormation — minimal CloudFront distribution skeleton
snippet.code:
Resources:
  AppDistribution:
    Type: AWS::CloudFront::Distribution
    Properties:
      DistributionConfig:
        Enabled: true
        Comment: SPA static assets
        DefaultCacheBehavior:
          TargetOriginId: S3Origin
          ViewerProtocolPolicy: redirect-to-https
          CachePolicyId: 658327ea-f89d-4fab-a63d-7e88639e58f6  # CachingOptimized managed
        Origins:
          - Id: S3Origin
            DomainName: !GetAtt AppBucket.RegionalDomainName
            S3OriginConfig:
              OriginAccessIdentity: ''  # use OAC in production — see cloudfront-s3 topic
        PriceClass: PriceClass_100  # US, Canada, Europe — cheaper than global
snippet.explanation: Distribution ties a default cache behavior to an S3 origin. PriceClass limits PoP regions for cost. Production adds OAC, custom domain, and path behaviors.

snippet.label: CLI — create invalidation when you must purge (prefer versioning instead)
snippet.code:
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id E1234567890ABC \
  --paths '/assets/*' '/index.html'

# Check invalidation status
aws cloudfront get-invalidation \
  --distribution-id E1234567890ABC \
  --id I2J3K4L5M6N7O8
snippet.explanation: Invalidation removes objects from all edge caches. Costs apply after free tier. Versioned filenames (app.v2.js) avoid needing this on every deploy.

snippet.label: CloudFormation — CloudWatch alarm on low cache hit rate
snippet.code:
Resources:
  LowCacheHitAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Properties:
      AlarmName: cloudfront-low-cache-hit-rate
      MetricName: CacheHitRate
      Namespace: AWS/CloudFront
      Statistic: Average
      Period: 300
      EvaluationPeriods: 2
      Threshold: 70
      ComparisonOperator: LessThanThreshold
      Dimensions:
        - Name: DistributionId
          Value: !Ref AppDistribution
      AlarmActions:
        - !Ref OpsTopic
snippet.explanation: CacheHitRate below 70% on a static site often means TTL misconfiguration, query-string cache busting, or missing compression. Alarm before origin costs spike.

blocks.title: CDN vs browser and framework caching
rows: Shared across all users at edge PoP
Per-user browser cache or platform edge
Cache-Control headers, ISR revalidate in Next.js
Wrong cache key leaks responses between users
Same risk if CDN caches Set-Cookie responses

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Caching POST responses or API JSON with TTL > 0 and no user in the cache key. Making S3 public instead of OAC because 'CDN needs access.' Running /* invalidation on every deploy instead of content-hashed bundles. Assuming CDN replaces horizontal scaling for write-heavy APIs.

blocks.text: Edge caches are eventually consistent — a deploy in us-east-1 does not instantly disappear from every PoP until TTL expires or you invalidate. Origin Shield (optional per origin) adds a regional mid-tier cache so 400+ edges do not all hammer S3 on a cold start. How to prove it in production: CloudWatch CacheHitRate and OriginRequests on the distribution; access logs with x-edge-result-type Hit vs Miss; curl -sI from multiple regions. PriceClass and geo restriction trade cost against coverage.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Extra per-GB charge in shield region
TTL 0 means no origin offload for dynamic paths

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'CDN makes everything faster' without naming cacheability, TTL, or cache keys. Strong answer: CDN reduces latency and origin load for cacheable GET/HEAD content; dynamic and authenticated paths need explicit TTL 0 and correct forwarded headers.

interviewTakeaways: A CDN caches responses at edge PoPs near users; on a miss it fetches from origin once and reuses the copy.
Do not cache personalized or authenticated responses unless the cache key includes the distinguishing header or cookie.
In production, watch CloudFront CacheHitRate and OriginRequests; versioned filenames beat mass invalidation.
60s: CDN = closer bytes + origin shield. Cache only safe GETs. OAC for private S3. TTL and cache keys matter more than PoP count.
Follow-up: how does Origin Shield change the miss path, and when is CloudFront the wrong tool?
commonPitfalls: Saying CDN speeds up databases or POST APIs — that gets you rejected because writes and dynamic auth responses are not CDN problems.
Strong answer: name cache hit rate, TTL, cache key components, and what stays origin-only.
Making S3 public 'for CloudFront' instead of using Origin Access Control.
Invalidating /* on every deploy when webpack/vite already emit hashed chunk names.

jsTsCorrelations.note: fetch() respects Cache-Control in the browser only for that user. CloudFront is a shared cache — one user's hit can serve the next user unless Vary or cache key includes their auth header.

jsTsCorrelations.concept: Next.js static export on S3 + CloudFront
jsTsCorrelations.note: next build emits hashed _next/static chunks ideal for long CDN TTL. HTML pages need shorter TTL or stale-while-revalidate. Same pattern as Angular prerender output to S3.
